title: Cato's last night
hookLine: at Utica in 46 BCE, refusing Caesar's pardon, Cato reads Plato on the soul through the night, and his ending is told honestly, not as a model
last: CLEANTHES CARRIES WATER — CARRY THE WATER.

cards: Week five is called Rome's hard nights, and it begins with the hardest. A word before we start: today's story ends in a death, and it's told carefully. North Africa, the city of Utica.

Rome is tearing itself apart in civil war, and Julius Caesar has just won. On the losing side is Marcus Cato, a senator well-known for being honest to the point of stubbornness, who had fought Caesar for years.
Caesar is coming. And he is known for pardoning his enemies. Cato refuses to be pardoned.

teach.b: Our source is Plutarch, writing generations later. He tells us Cato spent that last day making sure everyone else got out: arranging ships, calming the townspeople, helping others escape or make their peace with Caesar.
That evening he had dinner with friends and argued philosophy, loudly, about whether only a good person is truly free.

teach.h: PLATO ON THE SOUL, LATE AT NIGHT.
teach.b: Then he went to his room and read Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue about the death of Socrates and the soul, late into the night. His son and his friends could see where his mind was going. They were frightened.
They stayed close. They pleaded with him. And before morning, Cato ended his own life.
Later Romans praised him for it, and some Stoics saw it as a free choice. This path doesn't tell it that way, and it isn't a model.

Many traditions, Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist and others, teach against taking one's own life, and modern understanding sees much more going on in a night like that: exhaustion, despair, a mind that has narrowed until only one door seems open.
What Plutarch's account does show, if you read it slowly, is the people around him.

teach.h: A SON AND FRIENDS WHO TRIED.
teach.b: A son and friends who noticed, who tried, who wanted him to stay.
That's the part to keep. Hard nights are real. The mind at 3am is not a reliable narrator.
It tells you the dark is permanent. It isn't.
Morning comes, and so do other doors. But you often can't see them alone. That's what people are for.

how: Many traditions ask people to reach out in despair and to watch over those who are struggling; today that includes crisis lines such as 988 in the US, open at any hour.

go to bed and hope for the best.
games.why: they noticed, they stayed close, and they pleaded. that's the part of the story to keep: reach out before morning.

practice: Sit, and picture the faces of one or two people you could call on a heavy night. If none comes easily, that's worth knowing, and it's okay: picture a helpline instead, a voice that's awake when you're awake.
Then let a second face come, someone who might be having a hard night of their own, and hold them gently in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Cato. A Roman senator's hard last night, and the people who tried to reach him before morning.

orig.note: Greek, psychē: soul, breath, life. The subject of Plato's Phaedo, the book Cato read that night; English psyche and psychology come from it.

carryVoice: Your line: reach out before morning. In the US you can call or text 988 at any hour, and wherever you are, there is someone to call. That's day twenty-nine.
